entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a stored account of facts or events, or the best result ever achieved; as a verb, to store sound, pictures or information so it can be used later.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable, and its second vowel is weak (REK-erd); the verb stresses the second, and its first vowel is weak (rih-KORD). Many two-syllable noun–verb pairs, such as *present*, *object* and *conduct*, follow this pattern. *Recorder* and *recording* keep the verb stress.
examples: She broke the school **record** for the mile last spring.
Is it OK if I **record** our conversation?
Your medical **records** will be sent to the new clinic.

drill.sentence: Did anyone **record** the speech? I'd like a **record** of what she promised.

mistake.wrong: Can you REK-erd the meeting? (/ˈrɛkɚd/ for the verb)
mistake.why: Learners use one stress for both forms; the verb stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a gift or the time now (also an adjective: *present at the meeting*); as a verb, to show or explain something to an audience, or to give something formally.
entries.usage: The noun and the adjective stress the first syllable, PREZ-unt; the verb stresses the second, and its first vowel becomes weak (prih-ZENT). *Presenter* keeps the verb stress, while *presentation* moves the main stress to *-TAY-*.
examples: I still need to buy a birthday **present** for my sister.
She'll **present** the new budget to the board on Friday.
All five children were **present** when the will was read.

drill.sentence: At the party, the kids will **present** Grandma with a **present** they made themselves.
drill.hint: *will present* is the verb (prih-ZENT); *a present* is the noun (PREZ-unt).

mistake.wrong: I'll PREZ-unt my plan. (/ˈprɛzənt/ for the verb)
mistake.why: Learners know the noun first and keep its stress; the verb stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a rise in amount, number or size; as a verb, to become larger or to make something larger.
entries.usage: The noun usually stresses the first syllable and the verb the second; *decrease* works the same way. The pattern is not absolute: some Americans also stress the verb on the first syllable, especially when they contrast it with *decrease*.
examples: There's been a sharp **increase** in rent this year.
The city plans to **increase** bus service on weekends.
Most employees will get a three percent pay **increase** in January.

drill.sentence: If ticket prices **increase** again, we'll see a big **increase** in complaints.

mistake.wrong: an in-KREESS in sales (/ɪnˈkris/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Learners use the verb stress everywhere; most Americans stress the noun on the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a planned piece of work with a clear goal; as a verb, to forecast something, to show an image on a surface, or to give an impression (*project confidence*).
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable, and Americans use the *ah* of *pot* (PRAH-jekt). The verb stresses the second syllable with a weak first vowel (pruh-JEKT), and *projection* and *projector* keep that stress.
examples: My team is starting a new **project** next month.
Analysts **project** that home prices will fall slightly next year.
Can you **project** the map onto the wall so everyone can see it?

drill.sentence: For her school **project**, she wants to **project** old family photos onto a big screen.

mistake.why: German *Projekt* stresses the second syllable; the English noun stresses the first, and only the verb stresses the second.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: The numbers 13 and 30, and the other pairs like them (14 and 40, up to 19 and 90), which listeners easily confuse.
entries.usage: *Thirteen* stresses *-teen*, with a clear *t* and a long *ee*; *thirty* stresses the first syllable, and in American speech its *t* is a quick flap, close to a *d*. Before a stressed noun, *-teen* numbers often move their stress forward (*THIR-teen DOL-lars*), so the clear *t* and the long *ee* are what really tell the two apart.
examples: My daughter turns **thirteen** next week.
The bus comes every **thirty** minutes, even on Sundays.
Did you say **fifteen** or **fifty**? The line is really bad.

drill.sentence: The tickets cost **thirty** dollars, not **thirteen**.
drill.hint: *thirty*: stress first, flap t; *thirteen*: stress on *-teen*, clear t.

mistake.wrong: THUR-teen /ˈθɝtin/ at the end of a sentence
mistake.why: With the stress on the first syllable, *thirteen* is easily heard as *thirty*; stress *-teen* and keep its *t* clear.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: A picture taken with a camera; the art or practice of taking such pictures; and the adjective for anything related to them.
entries.usage: The stress moves with the suffix: *photograph* stresses the first syllable, *photography* and *photographer* the second, and *photographic* the third, just before *-ic*. Every unstressed *o* weakens to a schwa, so *photography* begins with *fuh*, not *foh*.
examples: She framed an old **photograph** of her grandparents.
He's taking a **photography** class at the community college.
My aunt has an almost **photographic** memory for faces.

drill.sentence: I love **photography**, but I hate posing for a **photograph**.

mistake.why: Learners keep the stress of *photograph*; with *-y* and *-er* the stress moves to the second syllable.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: The economy is the system of money, trade and jobs in a place; *economic* means related to it, and *economics* is the subject that studies it.
entries.usage: *Economy*, *economist* and *economize* stress the second syllable (ih-KAH-), while *economic*, *economics* and *economical* stress the third, because *-ic* pulls the stress to the syllable just before it. In *economic* and *economics*, the first syllable can be *ek* or *eek*; both are standard.
examples: The local **economy** depends heavily on tourism.
She studied **economics** before going to law school.
The **economic** effects of the drought will last for years.

drill.sentence: Tourism is the biggest part of the island's **economy**, so the storm's **economic** impact was huge.

mistake.why: German *Ökonomie* stresses the last syllable, like many German nouns in *-ie*; English *economy* stresses the second, KAH.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: *Politics* is the activity of government or of gaining power within a group; *political* is its adjective; a *politician* is a person whose job is politics.
entries.usage: The stress moves right as the word grows: the first syllable in *politics*, the second in *political*, the third in *politician*, just before *-ian*. The *o* is a full *ah* when stressed and a weak *uh* when not, so *political* starts with *puh*.
examples: Office **politics** can be more tiring than the actual work.
Let's not get **political** at Thanksgiving dinner this year.
My neighbor ran for city council, but she says she's not a real **politician**.

drill.sentence: Before he became a **politician**, he taught **political** science at a community college.

mistake.why: German *Politik* stresses the last syllable; English *politics* stresses the first.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: To examine something in detail in order to understand it; the noun for this process; and the adjective for a person or method that works this way.
entries.usage: Three related words, three stress positions: the first syllable in *analyze* and *analyst*, the second in *analysis*, and the third in *analytical* and *analytics*, just before *-ic*. The plural *analyses* ends in *-seez*: uh-NAL-uh-seez.
examples: We'll **analyze** the survey results and share them next week.
The doctor sent my blood sample off for **analysis**.
She's very **analytical**, so she reads every review before buying anything.

drill.sentence: My brother likes to **analyze** every game, but his **analysis** is usually wrong.

mistake.why: Learners keep the first-syllable stress of *analyze*; *analysis* stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, forward movement or improvement toward a goal; as a verb, to move forward or develop over time.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable with the *ah* of *pot*; the verb stresses the second, with a weak first vowel. The verb is less common and a bit formal (*as the disease progresses*), and *progressive* and *progression* keep its stress. The noun is uncountable: *make progress*, not *a progress*.
examples: We're making good **progress** on the kitchen remodel.
Symptoms usually **progress** slowly over several years.
As the evening **progressed**, the speeches got longer and funnier.

drill.sentence: The disease can **progress** quickly, but doctors are making real **progress** with new treatments.

mistake.wrong: We made pruh-GRESS. (/prəˈɡrɛs/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Learners use the stress of *progressive* and *progression*; the noun stresses the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a legal agreement; as a verb, to become smaller or tighter, or to catch an illness.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable; the verb meaning *shrink* or *catch an illness* stresses the second (kun-TRAKT), and so does *contraction*. The business verb (*contract with a supplier*, *contract out the cleaning*) is often stressed on the first syllable, like the noun.
examples: Read the **contract** carefully before you sign it.
Metal **contracts** as it cools.
He **contracted** malaria while traveling in West Africa.

drill.sentence: Under the new **contract**, workers who **contract** an illness on the job get extra sick days.
drill.hint: Noun first (KAHN-trakt), then the verb meaning *catch* (kun-TRAKT).

mistake.why: German *Kontrakt* stresses the second syllable; the English noun stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a physical thing, or the goal of an activity; as a verb, to say that you disagree with or oppose something.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable with the *ah* of *pot*; the verb stresses the second, and its first vowel is a weak *uh*. The verb is usually *object to* + noun or *-ing*, and *objection* and *objective* keep its stress (ub-JEK-tiv).
examples: Airport security found a sharp metal **object** in his bag.
The **object** of the game is to collect all the cards.
Several neighbors **objected** to the new parking rules.

drill.sentence: Does anyone **object** if I move this heavy **object** off the table?

mistake.why: German *Objekt* is usually stressed on the second syllable; the English noun stresses the first, and only the verb stresses the second.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, the way someone behaves, especially in a formal or professional setting; as a verb, to carry out an activity, to lead an orchestra, or to let heat or electricity pass through.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable (KAHN-dukt) and is formal: *code of conduct*, *professional conduct*. The verb stresses the second, with a weak first vowel (kun-DUKT), and *conductor* keeps that stress.
examples: The company fired him for unprofessional **conduct**.
Police are **conducting** an investigation into the fire.
Copper **conducts** electricity very well.

drill.sentence: The school will **conduct** a review of the coach's **conduct** during the game.

mistake.wrong: We'll KAHN-dukt a survey. (/ˈkɑnˌdʌkt/ for the verb)
mistake.why: Learners use the noun stress for both forms; the verb stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a clear difference between two things; as a verb, to compare things to show how they differ, or to be clearly different from something.
entries.usage: The noun always stresses the first syllable. The verb traditionally stresses the second (kun-TRAST), but many Americans also say KAHN-trast for the verb, so this pair is less strict than *record* or *object*. *In contrast* and *by contrast* use the noun stress.
examples: The **contrast** between the two brothers is striking.
The white walls make a nice **contrast** with the dark wood floors.
Her calm reply **contrasted** sharply with his angry email.

drill.sentence: If you **contrast** the two photos, the **contrast** in color is obvious.
drill.hint: The verb is often kun-TRAST; the noun is always KAHN-trast.

mistake.why: German *Kontrast* stresses the second syllable; the English noun always stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, an official document that allows you to do something; as a verb, to allow something, usually in formal language.
entries.usage: The noun usually stresses the first syllable (*a parking permit*, *a work permit*); the verb stresses the second, with a weak first vowel. The verb is formal and common in rules and signs (*Smoking is not permitted*), and in the fixed phrase *weather permitting*.
examples: You need a **permit** to park on this street overnight.
The building rules don't **permit** dogs over thirty pounds.
We'll eat outside, weather **permitting**.

drill.sentence: The city won't **permit** construction until you show them a valid **permit**.

mistake.wrong: a parking per-MIT (/pɚˈmɪt/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Learners know the verb from *permission* and keep its stress; Americans usually stress the noun on the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, fresh fruit and vegetables sold in stores; as a verb, to make, grow or create something.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable (PROH-doos or PRAH-doos); the verb stresses the second, with a weak first vowel. In the US there is usually no *y* sound after the *d*: -DOOS, not -DYOOS. Stores have a *produce section* or *produce aisle*, and *producer* keeps the verb stress.
examples: The **produce** section is at the back of the store.
This farm **produces** most of the strawberries sold in the state.
The film was **produced** on a tiny budget.

drill.sentence: Local farms **produce** most of the **produce** we sell in the summer.

mistake.wrong: the pruh-DOOS aisle (/prəˈdus/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Learners know *produce* mainly as a verb; the food noun stresses the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a person thought to be guilty of a crime; as a verb, to think that something is probably true, often something bad.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable, and so does the adjective (*The timing is suspect*); the verb stresses the second, with a weak first vowel (suh-SPEKT). *Suspicious* and *suspicion* also stress the second syllable.
examples: Police arrested a **suspect** near the train station.
I **suspect** she already knows about the surprise party.
The timing of his sick day seems a little **suspect** to me.

drill.sentence: Detectives **suspect** that the main **suspect** had help from a friend.

mistake.wrong: I SUS-pekt he's lying. (/ˈsʌˌspɛkt/ for the verb)
mistake.why: Learners use one stress for both forms; the verb stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a set of questions asked to many people, or a careful study of an area; as a verb, to look carefully at something as a whole, or to ask people questions.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable. The verb is traditionally sur-VAY, especially for *look over carefully* (*She surveyed the room*), but many Americans also say SUR-vay for the verb meaning *ask people questions*. In both forms, the last syllable keeps a full *ay*.
examples: Please take a few minutes to fill out our customer **survey**.
She stood at the door and **surveyed** the damage.
We **surveyed** two thousand parents about their kids' screen time.

drill.sentence: After the storm, officials came to **survey** the damage and asked us to fill out a **survey**.

mistake.wrong: fill out a sur-VAY (/sɚˈveɪ/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Learners use the verb stress for the noun; Americans stress the noun on the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, a quality or feature that someone or something has; as a verb, to say that something was caused or created by a particular person or thing.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable and ends in a full *byoot*; the verb stresses the second, starts with a weak *uh*, and its ending is often reduced (uh-TRIB-yut). The verb is almost always *attribute A to B*.
examples: Patience is an important **attribute** in a good teacher.
Doctors **attribute** the rise in injuries to electric scooters.
The power outage was later **attributed** to a squirrel chewing through a cable.

drill.sentence: The coach **attributes** the team's success to one **attribute** above all: discipline.

mistake.why: German *Attribut* stresses the last syllable; the English noun stresses the first, and the verb the second.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, what is inside something, or what a text, course or website contains; as an adjective, satisfied and not wanting more.
entries.usage: The noun stresses the first syllable (*online content*, *the contents of a box*); the adjective stresses the second, with a weak first vowel. The adjective usually comes after a verb (*I'm content with that*, *content to wait*); before a noun, people say *contented*: *a contented cat*.
examples: The **content** of the course is great, but the lectures are dull.
The **contents** of the box spilled all over the floor.
He seems perfectly **content** to stay home on weekends.

drill.sentence: I'm **content** with the design, but the **content** still needs a lot of work.

mistake.wrong: I'm KAHN-tent with my job. (/ˈkɑnˌtɛnt/ for the adjective)
mistake.why: Learners know the noun from phrases like *content creator*; the adjective stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, the details of where someone lives or can be reached, or a formal speech; as a verb, to deal with a problem, to speak to a group, or to write details on an envelope.
entries.usage: In the US the noun meaning *where you live* or *email address* is very often AD-dress, with stress on the first syllable; uh-DRESS for this noun is also common in the US and is the normal British form. The verb stresses the second syllable, and the noun meaning *a formal speech* often does too.
examples: What's your new **address**? I want to send you a card.
The mayor will **address** the crowd after the parade.
We need to **address** the noise problem before the neighbors complain.

drill.sentence: Before you **address** the envelope, double-check her new **address**.
drill.hint: Verb first (uh-DRESS), then the noun (US: AD-dress).

mistake.wrong: We need to AD-dress this issue. (/ˈæˌdrɛs/ for the verb)
mistake.right: We need to uh-DRESS this issue. /əˈdrɛs/
mistake.why: Learners extend the American noun stress to the verb; the verb stresses the second syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: As a noun, careful study to discover new facts; as a verb, to study a subject carefully, or to look for information before making a decision.
entries.usage: In the US both REE-surch and rih-SURCH are standard for the noun and the verb, and many speakers use both; REE-surch is especially common for the noun (*research funding*). Whichever stress you choose, the *s* is a sharp *s*, not a *z*, and *-search* has the r-colored vowel of *her*.
examples: **Research** shows that kids who read for fun do better in school.
I always **research** a car carefully before I buy it.
Our neighbor does cancer **research** at the university hospital.

drill.sentence: Before our trip to Japan, I spent hours doing **research** on train passes.
drill.hint: REE-surch or rih-SURCH; a sharp s, and the vowel of *her*.

mistake.why: German speakers often voice an *s* before a vowel, as in *Sonne* and *Rose*; in *research* it stays the voiceless *s* of *search*.

entries.label: -ate: noun vs. verb
entries.meaning: As a noun, a rough calculation, or a written statement of what a job will probably cost; as a verb, to calculate something roughly.
entries.usage: Both forms stress the first syllable; the difference is the ending. The noun ends in a weak *-mit*, while the verb ends in a full *-mayt* with a secondary stress. The same contrast appears in *approximate*, *duplicate*, *graduate* and *delegate*.
examples: The contractor gave us an **estimate** of twenty thousand dollars.
Experts **estimate** that the repairs will take two years.
At a rough **estimate**, about five hundred people showed up.

drill.sentence: Can you **estimate** how long the job will take and then put the **estimate** in writing?

mistake.why: Learners use the verb ending for the noun; the noun's last syllable is weak.

entries.label: -ate: noun vs. verb
entries.meaning: As a noun, a person who publicly supports a cause or speaks for others; as a verb, to publicly support or recommend something.
entries.usage: Both stress the first syllable; the noun ends in a weak *-kit*, the verb in a full *-kayt*. The verb takes a direct object or *-ing* (*advocate stricter rules*), and *advocate for* is also common in the US. Unlike German *Advokat*, the English noun is not the everyday word for a lawyer.
examples: She's a strong **advocate** for patients' rights.
Many doctors **advocate** walking at least thirty minutes a day.
Parents have been **advocating** for a crosswalk near the school.

drill.sentence: As a longtime **advocate** for cyclists, he **advocates** building more bike lanes.

mistake.wrong: a patient AD-vuh-kayt (/ˈædvəˌkeɪt/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Learners give the noun the full *-ate* of the verb; the noun ends in a weak *-kit*.

entries.label: -ate: adjective vs. verb
entries.meaning: As an adjective, not joined or connected, or different; as a verb, to divide things or people, or to move apart.
entries.usage: Both stress the first syllable. The adjective usually has two syllables and a weak end (SEP-rit, or SEP-uh-rit in careful speech), while the verb has three and ends in a full *-rayt*. The adverb *separately* follows the adjective: SEP-rit-lee.
examples: The kids finally have **separate** bedrooms.
**Separate** the egg whites from the yolks.
The couple **separated** after ten years of marriage.

drill.sentence: Please **separate** the recycling and put the glass in a **separate** bin.

mistake.wrong: two SEP-uh-rayt rooms (/ˈsɛpəˌreɪt/ for the adjective)
mistake.why: Learners use the full verb ending for the adjective; the adjective ends in a weak *-rit*.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: A *democracy* is a system of government by the people or their elected representatives; *democratic* is its adjective; a *democrat* is a person who supports it.
entries.usage: The stress is on the first syllable in *democrat*, the second in *democracy* and the third in *democratic*, just before *-ic*. The vowels change with it: *-moc-* is a full *MAH* in *democracy* but a weak *uh* in the other two. *Democratize* follows *democracy*: dih-MAH-kruh-tyze.
examples: Switzerland is a direct **democracy**, so voters decide many issues themselves.
The club made a **democratic** decision: everyone voted on the new logo.
He was a lifelong **democrat** who believed every adult should have a vote.

drill.sentence: Our book club is a real **democracy**: every choice is made by a **democratic** vote.

mistake.why: German *Demokratie* stresses the last syllable; English *democracy* stresses the second, MAH.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: A *hypothesis* is an idea proposed as a possible explanation, to be tested; *hypothetical* describes something imagined rather than real.
entries.usage: *Hypothesis* stresses the second syllable; *hypothetical* stresses the third, just before *-ical*. Both start with *high*, and the *th* is the voiceless sound of *think*. The plural *hypotheses* ends in *-seez*: hy-PAH-thuh-seez.
examples: Our **hypothesis** was that kids sleep better without screens in the bedroom.
Let me ask you a **hypothetical** question: what would you do with a million dollars?
Detectives are working on the **hypothesis** that the fire started in the kitchen.

drill.sentence: That's just a **hypothetical** example; it doesn't prove your **hypothesis**.

mistake.why: German *Hypothese* stresses the third syllable; English *hypothesis* stresses the second.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: *Statistics* are numbers that describe facts, and also the science of collecting and analyzing such numbers; a *statistician* is an expert in that science.
entries.usage: *Statistics* and *statistical* stress the second syllable, and their first vowel is a weak *uh*. *Statistician* moves the stress to the syllable just before *-ian* (STISH), and its first syllable becomes a full *stat*.
examples: Crime **statistics** for the city were released on Monday.
My cousin works as a **statistician** for a baseball team.
**Statistically**, you're safer on a plane than in a car.

drill.sentence: My sister became a **statistician** because she loved sports **statistics** as a kid.

mistake.why: Learners keep the stress of *statistics*; *-ian* pulls the stress to the syllable just before it.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: An *academy* is a school for special training or a society of experts; *academic* relates to schools and scholarship; *academia* is the world of universities and research.
entries.usage: The stress moves from the second syllable in *academy* to the third in *academic* (before *-ic*) and in *academia*. The vowel changes too: the stressed *-dem-* is a short *DEM* in *academic* but a long *DEE* in *academia*.
examples: She trained at a police **academy** in Texas.
My son's **academic** year starts in late August.
He left **academia** after his postdoc to work at a startup.

drill.sentence: After ten years in **academia**, she now runs a small music **academy** for kids.

mistake.why: Learners keep the short vowel of *academic*; in *academia* the stressed vowel is a long *ee*.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: *Specific* means exact and particular; to *specify* is to state something exactly; *specificity* is the quality of being exact, or, for a medical test, how well it avoids false positives.
entries.usage: *Specific* stresses the second syllable, just before *-ic*; *specify* stresses the first; *specificity* stresses the third (FIS), just before *-ity*. The first vowel is a weak *uh* in *specific* but a full *SPES* in the other two.
examples: Can you be more **specific** about what went wrong?
Please **specify** your shirt size when you order.
The new test has high **specificity**, so false positives are rare.

drill.sentence: The form asks you to **specify** a date, so be as **specific** as you can.

mistake.why: Learners keep the stress of *specific*; before *-ity* the stress moves to the syllable just before the ending.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: *Industry* is the production of goods, or a particular branch of business; *industrial* describes things connected with factories and production.
entries.usage: *Industry* stresses the first syllable, and its middle vowel is weak (IN-duh-stree). *Industrial* and *industrious* (hard-working) stress the second syllable, where the vowel becomes a full *uh*, as in *bus*.
examples: She's worked in the music **industry** for twenty years.
The old **industrial** area by the river is now full of restaurants and lofts.
Tourism is the island's biggest **industry**.

drill.sentence: The town's main **industry** used to be steel, and you can still see the old **industrial** buildings.

mistake.why: German *Industrie* and French *industrie* stress the last syllable; English *industry* stresses the first.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: *Energy* is the strength to be active, or power from sources such as electricity or fuel; *energetic* means full of energy and activity.
entries.usage: *Energy* stresses the first syllable, and the *g* is soft, like the *j* in *jet*. *Energetic* moves the stress to the syllable just before *-ic*: en-er-JET-ik.
examples: I don't have the **energy** to cook tonight.
Solar **energy** now powers most of the homes on our street.
Our new puppy is so **energetic** that he wears out the kids.

drill.sentence: Coffee gives me **energy**, but too much makes me jittery rather than **energetic**.
drill.hint: EN-er-jee, but en-er-JET-ik; the g is soft.

mistake.why: German *Energie* stresses the last syllable and has a hard *g*; English stresses the first syllable and uses a soft *g*.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: A *method* is a particular way of doing something; *methodical* means careful and well organized; *methodology* is the set of methods used in a field or a study.
entries.usage: *Method* stresses the first syllable and ends in a weak *-ud*; the *th* is the voiceless sound of *think*. *Methodical* stresses the second syllable (before *-ical*), and *methodology* the third (before *-ology*).
examples: My grandmother had her own **method** for making perfect rice.
She's very **methodical**; she plans every trip down to the hour.
Reviewers questioned the study's **methodology**.

drill.sentence: There's no single best **method**; just be **methodical** and patient.

mistake.why: German *Methode* stresses the second syllable and has a plain *t*; English *method* stresses the first and uses the *th* of *think*.

entries.label: stress shift
entries.meaning: A *category* is a group of things with shared features; *categorical* means relating to categories, or, of a statement, absolute and without any doubt.
entries.usage: *Category* stresses the first syllable and keeps a secondary stress on *-gor-*, so Americans say four clear syllables (British speakers often say three: KAT-uh-gree). *Categorical* moves the main stress to *-gor-*, while *categorize* keeps it on the first syllable: KAT-uh-guh-ryze.
examples: The film won in the best documentary **category**.
We sorted the donated books into **categories** by age.
The company issued a **categorical** denial of the rumors.

drill.sentence: The judge gave a **categorical** answer: the dog can't compete in that **category**.

mistake.why: German *Kategorie* stresses the last syllable; English *category* stresses the first.

entries.term: compound nouns: a greenhouse vs. a green house
entries.label: compound stress
entries.meaning: A *greenhouse* is a glass building for growing plants; *a green house* is simply a house painted green. The stress tells the listener which one you mean.
entries.usage: A compound noun stresses its first part: a GREEN-house, a BLACK-board, a HOT dog (the food). Adjective + noun stresses the noun: a green HOUSE, a black BOARD, a hot DOG (a dog that feels hot). The same contrast separates *a blackbird* (a kind of bird) from *a black bird* (any bird that is black).
examples: We grow tomatoes in a small **greenhouse** behind the garage.
They live in the **green house** on the corner, next to the school.
At the ballpark, I always get a **hot dog** and a lemonade.

drill.sentence: The **greenhouse** is behind the **green house** with the white fence.
drill.hint: Compound: GREEN-house; adjective + noun: green HOUSE.

mistake.wrong: a green HOUSE for growing tomatoes
mistake.why: With the stress on *house*, listeners hear a house that is painted green; the building for plants stresses *green*.

entries.term: phrasal verb vs. noun: set up / a setup
entries.label: phrasal verb stress
entries.meaning: *Set up* (verb) means to prepare or arrange something; *a setup* (noun) is the way something is arranged, or a trick that makes someone look guilty.
entries.usage: Phrasal verbs usually stress the particle: *set UP*, *work OUT*, *log IN*. The nouns made from them stress the first part and are often written as one word: *a SET-up*, *a WORK-out*, *a LOG-in*. When a pronoun comes between the parts, the particle keeps the stress: *set it UP*.
examples: We need to **set up** the chairs before the guests arrive.
My home office **setup** is just a laptop and a kitchen chair.
I do a quick **workout** before breakfast, and on weekends I **work out** at the gym.

drill.sentence: It took an hour to **set up** the new TV, but I love the **setup**.

mistake.wrong: Let's SET up the room. (stress on *set*)
mistake.why: Learners stress the verb part; in a phrasal verb the particle normally carries the main stress.

entries.label: initialism stress
entries.meaning: Initialisms are abbreviations read as separate letters, such as *FBI*, *CEO*, *DNA* and *USA*.
entries.usage: When an initialism stands alone or ends a phrase, the main stress falls on the last letter: the ef-bee-EYE, a see-ee-OH, dee-en-AY. Before a stressed noun the stress often moves to the first letter (*an FBI agent*: EF-bee-eye AY-junt). Acronyms read as words, like *NASA*, follow normal word stress.
examples: She worked for the **FBI** for twenty years.
The **CEO** announced the layoffs in a short email.
My doctor ordered an **MRI** of my knee.

drill.sentence: My neighbor just retired from the **FBI**, and his wife is a **CEO**.
drill.hint: Stress the last letter: ef-bee-EYE, see-ee-OH.

mistake.wrong: the EF-bee-eye, with the stress on the first letter
mistake.why: Learners give each letter equal weight or stress the first one; English puts the main stress on the last letter when the initialism stands alone.

entries.label: suffix stress rule
entries.meaning: Nouns ending in *-tion* or *-sion*, such as *information*, *explanation* and *decision*, follow a reliable stress rule.
entries.usage: The stress falls on the syllable just before *-tion* or *-sion*, so it often moves away from the base word: *inFORM* becomes *inforMAtion*, and *exPLAIN* becomes *explaNAtion*. The vowel can change too: the stressed *ay* of *explain* becomes a weak *uh* in *explanation*. A common exception is *television*, which Americans stress on the first syllable: TEL-uh-vizh-un.
examples: Can you send me more **information** about the apartment?
Her **explanation** of the bill made everything clear.
It was a tough **decision**, but we decided to sell the car.

drill.sentence: Thanks for the **explanation**; that **information** really helps.
drill.hint: Stress the syllable just before -tion: NAY, MAY.

mistake.why: German *Information* and French *information* stress the ending; in English *-tion* is a weak *-shun*, and the stress falls just before it.

entries.label: suffix stress rule
entries.meaning: Nouns ending in *-ity*, such as *personality*, *university* and *possibility*, follow a reliable stress rule.
entries.usage: The stress falls on the syllable just before *-ity*, so it often moves away from the base word: *PERsonal* becomes *persoNALity*, and *PUBlic* becomes *pubLICity*. In American speech the *t* of *-ity* is a quick flap, so the ending sounds like *-uh-dee*.
examples: My brother has a big **personality**, and he loves a crowd.
She got into a **university** in California on a full scholarship.
There's a real **possibility** of snow this weekend.

drill.sentence: The **university** hired a guide with a big **personality** for its campus tours.
drill.hint: Stress the syllable just before -ity: VUR, NAL.

mistake.why: German *Universität* stresses the last syllable; in English the stress falls just before *-ity*.

entries.label: -ment stress
entries.meaning: Common nouns ending in *-ment* whose German relatives (*Dokument*, *Instrument*, *Argument*) are stressed differently.
entries.usage: These nouns stress the first syllable, and *-ment* is a weak *-munt* that is never stressed. The verb *document* has the same stress but a fuller ending (DAHK-yuh-ment). Longer forms move the stress onto *-men-*: *documentary*, *instrumental*, *argumentative*.
examples: Please sign the **document** on page three.
She plays three **instruments**, including the cello.
We had a silly **argument** about whose turn it was to cook.

drill.sentence: The **argument** started when someone spilled coffee on an important **document**.
drill.hint: Stress the first syllable; -ment is weak.

mistake.why: German *Dokument* stresses the last syllable; the English noun stresses the first, and *-ment* is weak.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: To *develop* is to grow, change or build something over time; *development* is the process or a result of it, such as a new housing area.
entries.usage: Both stress the second syllable, and the stress does not move when *-ment* is added; *developer* and *developing* keep it too. The last syllable of *develop* is a weak *-up*, and American spelling has no final *e*.
examples: It takes years to **develop** a new medicine.
There's a new housing **development** going up near the lake.
Kids **develop** language skills very fast before age five.

drill.sentence: The city plans to **develop** the old rail yard, but the **development** won't start until next year.
drill.hint: Stress the second syllable in both: dih-VEL.

mistake.wrong: dih-VEL-ahp /dɪˈvɛlɑp/, with a full *o* as in *top*
mistake.why: Learners read the *o* as written; the unstressed last syllable is a weak *-up*, also in *development* and *developer*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: To explain or decide what something means; also, to translate spoken words from one language into another while people are speaking.
entries.usage: *Interpret* and *interpreter* stress the second syllable, and the last syllable of *interpret* is weak (-prit). *Interpretation* moves the main stress to *-TAY-*, just before *-tion*, and *-ter-* keeps a secondary stress.
examples: How do you **interpret** his silence?
She works as a court **interpreter** for Spanish speakers.
There are many **interpretations** of the poem's ending.

drill.sentence: My grandmother doesn't speak English, so my cousin will **interpret** for her at the doctor's.
drill.hint: Stress on the second syllable: in-TUR-prit.

mistake.why: German *Interpret* and *interpretieren* stress a later syllable; English *interpret* stresses the second.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A group of people chosen to make decisions or do a particular job for a larger organization.
entries.usage: Three syllables with stress on the middle one and a weak first vowel (*kuh*). In American speech the double *t* is a quick flap, so it sounds close to kuh-MID-ee. *Commit* and *commitment* stress the same syllable.
examples: The hiring **committee** meets on Thursday.
She's on the **committee** that's planning the school fundraiser.
A city **committee** approved the new bike lanes.

drill.sentence: My dad joined the neighborhood **committee** that organizes the Fourth of July picnic.

mistake.why: German *Komitee* and French *comité* stress the last syllable; English stresses the middle one.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: To *contribute* is to give money, time or ideas as part of a shared effort; to *distribute* is to hand out or spread something among people or places.
entries.usage: In the US both verbs stress the second syllable, and the first vowel is weak: kun-TRIB-yoot, dih-STRIB-yoot. KAHN-truh-byoot and DIS-truh-byoot are heard in British English and sound British in the US. *Contribution* and *distribution* move the stress to *-BYOO-*, just before *-tion*.
examples: Everyone **contributed** ten dollars toward her gift.
The food bank **distributes** meals to about three hundred families a week.
She **contributes** a lot in meetings, even though she's new.

drill.sentence: Volunteers will **distribute** flyers, and local shops will **contribute** prizes.
drill.hint: US: stress the second syllable, STRIB and TRIB.

mistake.why: This is a British variant; Americans stress the second syllable, as in the verb *attribute*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A series of actions or steps that lead to a result; as a verb, to deal with something in a set way, such as a request or an application.
entries.usage: Americans stress the first syllable and usually use the *ah* of *pot* (PRAH-sess); PROH-sess is also heard in the US and is common in Canada and Britain. The noun and the usual verb sound the same. The plural *processes* is normally PRAH-sess-iz; PRAH-sess-eez is heard too, but some listeners dislike it.
examples: Applying for a visa is a slow **process**.
Our bank can **process** your loan in two days.
Grief is a **process**, and it takes as long as it takes.

drill.sentence: The whole **process** of buying a house took almost four months.
drill.hint: Stress on the first syllable; US vowel as in *pot*.

mistake.why: German *Prozess* stresses the second syllable; the English noun and verb stress the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A person you work with, especially in a profession or an organization.
entries.usage: Two syllables with stress on the first: the first vowel is the *ah* of *pot*, and the end rhymes with *league*, with a silent *-ue*. The word is fairly formal; in casual American speech, people often say *coworker*.
examples: A **colleague** of mine recommended this restaurant.
She's well liked by her **colleagues** at the hospital.
I'd like you to meet my **colleague**, Dr. Patel.

drill.sentence: My wife and her **colleague** carpool to work every day.

mistake.why: German *Kollege* and French *collègue* stress the second syllable; English stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A set of official rules for how something must be done, or the formal rules of behavior on official occasions.
entries.usage: Three syllables with stress on the first and a secondary stress on the last. The middle *o* is a weak *uh*, and the end varies between *-kawl*, *-kahl* and *-kohl*; all of them are standard.
examples: The lab follows a strict **protocol** for handling blood samples.
If the alarm goes off, follow the fire **protocol** and leave by the stairs.
The hospital changed its **protocol** for visitors during flu season.

drill.sentence: Diplomatic **protocol** decides who sits next to the guest of honor at a state dinner.
drill.hint: Stress on the first syllable: PROH.

mistake.why: German *Protokoll* stresses the last syllable; English stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A room or building equipped for scientific experiments, tests or research.
entries.usage: Americans stress the first syllable and keep a secondary stress on *-tor-*: LAB-ruh-tor-ee, usually with four syllables. The British say luh-BOR-uh-tree, with stress on the second syllable. In everyday speech most people just say *lab*.
examples: She runs a **laboratory** that studies sleep in mice.
The blood samples were sent to a state **laboratory** for testing.
For a few years, my brother turned the garage into a kind of **laboratory**.

drill.sentence: The police **laboratory** confirmed that the paint matched the car.
drill.hint: US: stress the first syllable, LAB.

mistake.why: This is the British pattern; Americans stress the first syllable and keep the *-tor-*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: *Primarily* means mainly or mostly; *necessarily* means in a way that cannot be avoided, and is most common in *not necessarily* (not always).
entries.usage: Most Americans stress the *-ar-* syllable, which has a full *air* sound (PRY-mair-uh-lee, stressed on the first syllable, is also heard); *temporarily*, *ordinarily* and *voluntarily* work the same way. The adjectives keep their own stress (PRY-mair-ee, NES-uh-sair-ee). British speakers often stress the adverbs like the adjectives and shorten them: PRY-muh-ruh-lee.
examples: The app is used **primarily** by college students.
Expensive wine isn't **necessarily** better wine.
The trail is **temporarily** closed because of a rockslide.

drill.sentence: We moved here **primarily** for the schools, not **necessarily** for the weather.
drill.hint: US: stress the *-ar-* syllable: pry-MAIR, nes-uh-SAIR.

mistake.why: This shortened form is typical of British speech; Americans keep a full *air* and usually stress it.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: Holding your attention because it is unusual, exciting or worth thinking about.
entries.usage: Usually three syllables with stress on the first: the *-ter-* drops out, so it starts like *in-truh*. A four-syllable form with a light secondary stress on *-rest-* is also common, and many Americans drop the *t* after *n* (IN-er-es-ting). The main stress is never on *-rest-*.
examples: That's an **interesting** idea; tell me more.
The museum was more **interesting** than I expected.
It'll be **interesting** to see how the new coach handles the team.

drill.sentence: The most **interesting** part of the trip was a cooking class with a local family.
drill.hint: Stress the first syllable; usually three syllables, IN-truh-sting.

mistake.why: German *interessant* stresses a late syllable, and *-rest-* looks like a stressed word; English stresses the first syllable.
